own_scenes.desc: Richie Hawtin llegó con diez años de un pueblo inglés a Windsor, la ciudad canadiense al sur de Detroit, se volvió tímido y encontró en la música su forma de encajar: con dieciocho años ganó su noche, «Confusion», en el Shelter (el sótano del St. Andrew’s Hall), y llevó el techno a estudiantes y chavales de los suburbios, como Blake Baxter en el Majestic. Allí conoció a Kenny Larkin y a John Acquaviva, DJ de London (Ontario) nacido en Italia, conocido como «J’acquaviva +8» por su tono de plato preferido. Ignorados por Transmat, fundaron Plus 8 en 1990: «Elements of Tone» (States of Mind, con sonidos de un juguete Merlin) lo unió al bleep de Sheffield; «We Shall Overcome» de Larkin sampleaba a Martin Luther King. El sello «The Future Sound of Detroit» en la etiqueta blanca de «Technarchy» enfadó a la comunidad negra del techno (Hawtin y Acquaviva estaban entre los primeros artistas blancos de la zona, y aún coleaban los abusos del sello Paragon), pero el disco de Cybersonik (Hawtin y Daniel Bell) vendió veinte mil copias. Se sumaron Speedy J (Jochem Paap, Róterdam), V-Room, Sysex, Ken Ishii (UTU), Joey Beltram (Vortex) y Fred Gianelli; el recopilatorio From Our Minds to Yours (1991) fue el primer techno de la zona en vinilo, casete y CD. Asustados por el uso de «Thrash» en el Parkzicht de Róterdam, abandonaron la dureza: Hawtin pasó a F.U.S.E., Circuit Breaker y Plastikman, cuatro discos (1993-1998) de 303 lentas y atmosféricas con kas de más («Kriket», «Helikopter»), con Nova-Mute. Larkin, único artista negro del sello, se fue tras quedarse fuera de la gira de 1991.

refs.q: I just happened to get out an extra two dollars to get there. I didn’t see it as a different place.”
refs.para: For the white label of their third release later that year, the members of Plus 8 had the words “The Future Sound of Detroit” stamped in red on the back. But while they had intended this statement to project an idea of Detroit techno as a large regional sound, it ended up having the opposite effect—many Detroit artists felt that Plus 8 was cashing in on a reputation it hadn’t yet earned. “That’s why we had some problems when we started Plus 8,” says Hawtin. “It wasn’t that we were trying to jump onto that scene. . . . [Going to Detroit] was just like getting in my car and going down the street. . . . I just happened to get out an extra two dollars to get there. I didn’t see it as a different place.” The fact that Hawtin and Acquaviva were among the first white techno artists in the Detroit area didn’t help either, and the white label’s stamp raised the ire of Detroit’s African American techno community that, in general, remained suspicious of Plus 8 for years afterward.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Off to Battle: Redefining the Detroit Underground, 1990–1995

refs.q: When Dan [techno artist Daniel Bell] and I heard it, we said, “You know what? We sound as good as the records we buy!” We were so proud of ourselves.
refs.para: That one record really got the world interested. Richie [Hawtin] was already in top form as a DJ and he edited the song together. . . . We had done a handful of mixes and Richie took them, chopped them up, and said, “I’ve been to parties and this is going to work . . . this is how it should be.” When Dan [techno artist Daniel Bell] and I heard it, we said, “You know what? We sound as good as the records we buy!” We were so proud of ourselves.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Off to Battle: Redefining the Detroit Underground, 1990–1995

refs.q: We liked machine-driven music, but we didn’t like it so rigid—that was the difference with Detroit music.
refs.para: It was clear that Plus 8 wasn’t going to follow the degradation of “jack” to “jack-boot” and, stunned by the Parkzicht experience, the label backed away from Cybersonik’s sonic fury. “Those tracks [the harder ones like “Thrash”] sound really rigid now,” says Hawtin. “We liked machine-driven music, but we didn’t like it so rigid—that was the difference with Detroit music. None of us were making hard music just for the sake of it. . . . We weren’t slamming people over the head just for the sake of it. It was just intense.”
